worksheet.title: Match the Algorithm
worksheet.subtitle: Read the steps and name the job
worksheet.learning_goal: I can match an algorithm to the job its steps do.

parts.title: An algorithm does a job
parts.text: Every algorithm does a job. Read the steps and figure out the job. Match each algorithm to its job. One job has no algorithm — you will write it.

parts.title: What job is Algorithm 1?
parts.prompt: Read the steps. Which job does Algorithm 1 do? Write the job.

parts.title: What job is Algorithm 2?
parts.prompt: Which job does Algorithm 2 do? Write the job.

parts.title: You try — write the leftover one
parts.prompt: The leftover job is 'get a drink'. Write an algorithm for it — 3 or 4 steps in order, one per line.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: The steps of an algorithm tell you what job it does. Reading code to figure out what it does is a big part of being a coder.

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students read two algorithms, figure out the job each one does, and match it — then write the algorithm for the leftover job. Reading code to determine what it accomplishes is abstraction and a core part of C3.2; writing the missing algorithm is C3.1.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 1 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: cover the algorithm titles and have students guess the job from the steps alone.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: read Algorithm 1's steps. 'Wet, soap, rinse, dry — these steps wash your hands.'
2. WE DO: Exercise 1 — Algorithm 1 = wash hands. Exercise 2 — Algorithm 2 (bowl, scoop, put down, call) = feed the dog.
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — the leftover job is 'get a drink'; students write its steps (e.g. get a cup, turn on the tap, fill the cup, turn off the tap).
4. Connect: 'Coders read code to figure out what it does — the steps tell the job.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — Algorithm 1 = wash hands (wet, add soap, rinse, dry).
Ex 2 — Algorithm 2 = feed the dog (get the bowl, scoop the food, put it down, call the dog).
Ex 3 — get a drink: a sample algorithm is get a cup, turn on the tap, fill the cup, turn off the tap. Accept any 3-4 sensible ordered steps.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: matching by one word instead of the whole job — have students check that every step fits the job they chose.
Extend: ask students to write a 2-algorithm puzzle of their own for a partner to match.
Success indicator: the child matches Algorithm 1 to wash hands and Algorithm 2 to feed the dog, and writes a sensible 'get a drink' algorithm.
